Contents

1. Project intent and principles

  • Personal project, built to professional standard. Cost is not the driver and there is no deadline. Buying a comparable robot would be cheaper (Unitree's R1 starts at $5,900), so the reasons to build are the Hitmonlee form, owning the design, and what you learn.
  • Professional means disciplined, not prototype-free. CAD, drawings, BOM and revisions for every part; measured test data before each spend gate; prototypes are expected and budgeted.
  • Reproducible, not mass-producible. Unit #1 is defined so it can be rebuilt or repaired from the released CAD/BOM. It is not optimised for volume manufacturing.
  • Simulation first, then one joint, one leg, lower body, whole body. See the digital twin page.

2. Executive summary

Project Hitmonlee is a real humanoid whose mechanical structure, electronics, control stack and perception are designed as one system, with Hitmonlee as the physical form. It is a personal project built to a professional standard: nothing is improvised at the bench, and every part exists first as CAD, a drawing and a BOM line.

How it gets built

  1. Define the product digitally: requirements, CAD, URDF/MJCF twin, drawings, BOM, interfaces.
  2. Prove control in simulation before hardware exists.
  3. Test one actuator, then one joint, then one leg against the twin.
  4. Suppliers make the parts; you inspect, assemble and test them.
  5. Every measured failure becomes a CAD revision, not a workaround.

What it is not

Not an animatronic costume, not a hand-fabricated bracket build, and not a robot wrapped around a commercial platform. A comparable robot is cheaper to buy (Unitree's R1 starts at $5,900), so the reasons to build are the form, owning the design, and what you learn.

Core principle: you own the architecture and the engineering; suppliers provide manufacturing capability. The robot is defined by CAD, drawings, BOMs, interfaces and software.
Biggest risks: (1) the first actuator choice fixes geometry, power, thermals and ratios; (2) bipedal locomotion is the hardest software problem; (3) simulation only helps once it is calibrated against measured hardware. The gates in this plan exist to retire these three in order.

4. Why Hitmonlee

Hitmonlee is unusually suitable for a serious humanoid project because its body plan does not force wings, a shell, a quadrupedal torso or other mechanisms that dominate the engineering. The long-legged humanoid form gives us a direct path to a conventional bipedal architecture while leaving room for a deliberately mechanical aesthetic.

The Pokémon exterior should not be treated as a costume added at the end. The CAD skeleton should establish the silhouette, mounting points and cable routing so the final form remains mechanically honest.

5. Manufacturing philosophy

5.1 No home factory

Do not buy a CNC mill, lathe, welding setup or large 3D printer initially. Use one engineering/assembly base (the original plan assumed Hong Kong; see the open decisions) and Shenzhen as the manufacturing partner network.

5.2 Design → manufacture → inspect → test → revise

Requirements
   ↓
System architecture
   ↓
CAD + digital twin
   ↓
Engineering drawings + BOM
   ↓
Prototype quote (3–5 Shenzhen suppliers)
   ↓
Manufacture
   ↓
Incoming inspection
   ↓
Assembly
   ↓
Joint / limb / system tests
   ↓
Measured failure → CAD revision
   ↓
Revision-controlled re-manufacture

5.3 Structural materials

  • Primary: CNC-machined 6061-T6 aluminium for most structural parts.
  • Higher-stress / weight-sensitive parts: 7075-T6 aluminium selectively.
  • Steel: shafts, bearings, fasteners and wear interfaces.
  • Polymer/composite: covers, sensor windows, cosmetic shell and low-load components.

The important point is that Shenzhen receives parts, not a request to “make a robot.” Each part has a drawing, material, tolerance, finish and revision.

5.4 Hybrid manufacturing

  • Print first. A modest desktop FDM printer for fit-checks, cable routing, head/shell mock-ups and low-load parts before paying for aluminium.
  • Machined aluminium where it matters: legs, pelvis, torso, joint interfaces.
  • Cheaper stock forms elsewhere: laser-cut or waterjet plate, bent sheet, and tube with machined end fittings instead of fully pocketed 5-axis parts.
  • Batch orders: quote identical and left/right mirrored parts together; per-part price falls with quantity.
  • The release package (STEP, drawing, material, tolerance, finish, revision) is unchanged.

6. Mechanical architecture

6.1 Recommended DOF starting point

GroupDOFPurpose
Left leg6Hip 3 + knee 1 + ankle 2
Right leg6Hip 3 + knee 1 + ankle 2
Left arm4–5Shoulder 3 + elbow 1 + optional wrist
Right arm4–5Shoulder 3 + elbow 1 + optional wrist
Waist1–2Yaw initially; pitch optional
Neck2Yaw + pitch
Total23–26Final count determined after actuator selection

Do not lock the DOF count yet. The actuator catalogue, required torque, mass and desired manipulation capability should determine it.

Hands and the goal list. Grasping, placing and "retrieve cup" need a hand or gripper, and none is in the 23–26 DOF count. Decide before freezing the manipulation goals: gripper (adds DOF, mass, cost) or pointing/gesture-only.

6.2 Joint module

Each joint should be treated as a reusable engineering module:

BLDC motor
    ↓
gear reduction
    ↓
output bearing / shaft
    ↓
absolute encoder
    ↓
mechanical housing
    ↓
CAN/CAN-FD + power
    ↓
higher-level controller

An integrated actuator is the robot's muscle-and-joint package: motor, reduction, position sensing and usually motor electronics. The exact commercial actuator must be selected through a joint-level trade study rather than assuming a brand/model now.

6.3 Serviceability

  • Removable covers with captive/standard fasteners.
  • Replaceable actuator modules.
  • Internal cable channels and strain relief.
  • Defined connector locations.
  • No component should require destruction of another component for removal.
  • Every actuator and sensor should have a replaceable part number.

8. Software architecture

Use ROS 2 as the system integration layer, C++ for deterministic/high-rate robot components, and Python for research, perception and orchestration.

LayerLanguageResponsibilities
FirmwareC/C++motor driver interface, encoder reading, safety limits, watchdogs
Hardware abstractionC++CAN/CAN-FD, actuator state/command interfaces
Real-time controlC++joint control, whole-body control, balance
Kinematics/planningC++/PythonFK, IK, trajectory generation, footstep planning
PerceptionPython/C++camera pipelines, detection, pose, hands, depth
AI/behaviourPythontask planning, dialogue, high-level behaviour
Simulation/researchPythonMuJoCo, JAX, optimisation, RL experiments
UI/toolsPython/TypeScript optionaltelemetry, calibration, diagnostics

8.1 ROS 2 / ros2_control

Use ROS 2 Jazzy initially unless a later stable distribution becomes the better deployment target. ros2_control provides the hardware abstraction, controller manager, lifecycle and interfaces needed to make the same robot description work against real hardware and simulated hardware. Its controller manager connects controllers to hardware interfaces and manages the control loop. ros2_control documentation.

Implement a custom SystemInterface for the actuator bus. This should expose joint position, velocity and—if the actuator supports it—effort/torque state and command interfaces.

8.2 Motion planning

Use MoveIt 2 for manipulation and collision-aware arm motion rather than writing a complete planning stack from zero. MoveIt 2 supports kinematics, motion planning, 3D perception and planning scenes and integrates with ros2_control. MoveIt 2 documentation.

8.3 Core software modules

ModuleWhat you will build

hitmonlee_hardwareCAN/CAN-FD driver and ros2_control hardware interface.
hitmonlee_calibrationEncoder zeroing, camera calibration, IMU alignment, actuator calibration.
hitmonlee_stateRobot state estimation and sensor fusion.
hitmonlee_kinematicsFK/IK, Jacobians, body/foot transforms.
hitmonlee_controlJoint/whole-body control, impedance and balance.

hitmonlee_manipulationReach, grasp, place, point and arm coordination.

9. Perception system

The goal is not merely “eyes.” It is a robotic perception system that maintains a useful representation of the environment.

Recommended sensor layout

  • Head: stereo RGB cameras for person/object/hand perception.
  • Head depth: RGB-D/depth sensor for metric distance and manipulation.
  • Side/rear cameras: wide-angle coverage for navigation and people entering the scene.
  • IMU: high-rate orientation/acceleration.
  • Feet: contact/force sensing if feasible.
  • Joint encoders: joint state from every actuator.
  • Microphones: speech direction/voice interface.

Design all sensor mounts, apertures, cable channels and service access into the CAD before manufacturing.

Perception pipeline

Cameras / IMU
      ↓
timestamp + calibration
      ↓
image/depth processing
      ↓
person / object detection
      ↓
pose + hand landmarks
      ↓
multi-object tracking
      ↓
3D scene/world model
      ↓
task/behaviour layer

Hand signals should be treated as a specific perception subsystem: hand landmark extraction → temporal gesture classifier → confidence threshold → behaviour event.

10. Head, eyes and expression

Separate seeing from expressing.

Sensor bay (seeing)
  • Rigid head sub-frame carrying stereo RGB, depth camera, microphones and IMU if used.
  • Cameras sit at the eye positions behind a dark, smoked window cut to Hitmonlee's eye shape.
  • Camera extrinsics go into the URDF and MJCF from the first CAD release.
  • Cable channel through the 2-DOF neck with strain relief.
Expressive eyes (showing)
  • Two small round LCDs (a 1.28" SPI GC9A01-class panel is a common choice; verify) behind a shaped mask.
  • A small microcontroller (RP2040 or ESP32 class) drives them from behaviour events: blink, look-at (pupil offset from head pose), neutral, angry.
  • Cheap and easy to rework, and it keeps fragile parts away from the calibrated cameras.
  • Print head prototypes first.

11. Behaviour architecture

Do not connect a large language model directly to motor commands. Use a layered architecture:

Human / environment
        ↓
Perception
        ↓
World model
        ↓
Behaviour / task planner
        ↓
Validated robot skill
        ↓
Motion planner
        ↓
Whole-body controller
        ↓
Joint controllers
        ↓
Actuators

Example: human points at a cup → hand tracker estimates pointing ray → world model identifies cup → behaviour layer selects “retrieve cup” → manipulation planner generates reach trajectory → controller executes it within joint/force/safety constraints.

12. Control strategy

Each stage must pass in simulation and then on the rig before the next begins. Stages A–D are classical; stepping and walking use a learned policy inside a classical safety layer.

StageWhatDone when
A. Joint controlPosition and velocity tracking on every jointTracking error inside the limit you set (the render sheet suggests <2°)
B. ImpedanceCompliant joint behaviour for contact and disturbance recoveryStable under push and contact tests
C. State estimationFuse encoders, IMU and contact to estimate base pose, velocity and contact stateEstimate matches motion-capture or rig reference
D. StandingFind a stable posture in sim, reproduce on hardwareTethered, then unsupported stand
E. Weight shiftDeliberate centre-of-mass transfer between feetRepeatable shifts without stepping
F. SteppingRL policy trained in MJX with domain randomisation, checked sim-to-simSingle controlled steps on the tether
G. WalkingSlow walking, turning, stopping, disturbance recoverySlow free walking on a flat indoor floor
Safety layer (always on): joint, torque and thermal limits, watchdogs, fall detection and motor disable are classical code the policy cannot override. Pipeline details are on the digital twin page.

14. Engineering files sent to Shenzhen

Every manufactured part should have a release package containing:

  • STEP file
  • 2D manufacturing drawing PDF
  • material specification
  • critical dimensions and tolerances
  • surface finish
  • thread specifications
  • heat-treatment requirement where relevant
  • inspection requirements
  • part number + revision
  • quantity

For assemblies, maintain a BOM with manufacturer part numbers for bearings, fasteners, actuators, sensors and electronics. Keep supplier-specific alternatives documented rather than silently substituting components.

15. Sourcing

Leads only. I have not dealt with any of these companies; prices are listings seen in September 2026 and will change. Supplier pages are marketing.

Actuators

VendorNotes
CubeMars (AK / AKE / AKH)AK80-64: 120 Nm peak, 48 V, listed ~$890–990. AKH70-48: 222 Nm peak, 1.4 kg, 7 mm hollow bore for cables, dual CAN, ~$699. Buy direct and compare landed cost against retailers (one US retailer lists the AK80-64 at ~$1,151 with tariffs).

Bus voltage: the larger units above are 48 V class, so design battery, BMS, contactor and e-stop for that.

Machining and prototyping

TypeNames
Shenzhen shopsRJC (own factory, 100+ CNC machines), Shenzhen Alu Rapid Prototype (claims ISO 9001:2015), XTJ CNC (robotics page, 24-hour quotes), Shenzhen VMT Metal Product
Quote platformsRapidDirect and WayKen (Shenzhen), HLH Rapid (Shenzhen/Dongguan), Fictiv, Xometry, Protolabs. PCBWay and JLCCNC are also worth checking (not verified here).
Vetting protocol: send the same small test part with a proper drawing to 3–5 suppliers; ask for material certificates and an inspection report; measure the parts yourself; judge their DFM feedback; keep two and hold the rest in reserve. Do the same with 2–3 actuator samples before committing to a family.

Add a desktop FDM printer ($300–600) for fit-checks and non-structural parts. A large printer is still not required. Also budget a tether/gantry test rig (overhead support with a load cell if possible) before any standing tests.

17. Initial computer/software workstation

For development, use a Linux workstation with a capable NVIDIA GPU if possible. Isaac Sim is GPU-heavy; MuJoCo itself is much lighter. The Jetson Orin Nano Super is a cheap deployment/prototyping edge computer; NVIDIA lists it at $399 MSRP in current documentation. NVIDIA Jetson FAQ.

Reinforcement-learning training and Isaac Sim need a capable NVIDIA GPU workstation (roughly $2,500–4,000 if you don't already own one); this is separate from the onboard computer. Do not buy the final onboard computer yet. Build the robot's software against interfaces that allow simulation and desktop execution first.

The original envelope (~$10,500) was too low: it allowed about $4,000 for 20–24 actuators, while the 120 Nm-class hip/knee units alone list near $900 each. Revised for a 1.2–1.4 m, ~25 kg, machined-aluminium build on off-the-shelf actuators:

Lean path: applying the cost levers in §19 (per-joint actuator sizing, fewer DOF at first, printed non-structural parts, plate/tube links, batch orders, bench power) might bring the build to roughly $8–14k excluding the workstation and rig. That is my estimate, not a quote.

These are planning estimates, not supplier quotations. Actuators and machining should be quoted before committing to the final architecture.

19. Cost levers without lowering the standard

  1. Buy actuators direct from the manufacturer and ask for quantity pricing.
  2. Size actuators per joint; use the 100+ Nm class only at hips and knees.
  3. Print head, shell, covers, sensor housings and probably arm links.
  4. Consider printed cycloidal gearboxes for low-load joints (arms, neck), as Berkeley Humanoid Lite does; keep metal units in the legs.
  5. Use plate, tube and sheet links; reserve 5-axis CNC for joint interfaces.
  6. Batch identical and mirrored parts.
  7. Start with a 12-DOF lower body, a locked waist and simple arms; add DOF later.
  8. Begin sensing with one depth camera plus motor current; add foot force sensing later.
  9. Develop on a tether and bench supply; buy the battery late.
  10. Use a mini-PC or Jetson Orin Nano-class computer early.

Critical rule: do not order 24 actuators or the complete aluminium skeleton before the single-joint and single-limb gates have passed. The first actuator choice determines geometry, power, thermal management, joint ratios and much of the rest of the machine.

21. Safety architecture

  • Physical emergency-stop that removes actuator power.
  • Independent power cutoff/contactor.
  • Per-joint software position/velocity/current limits.
  • Actuator thermal limits.
  • Communication watchdog.
  • Heartbeat timeout.
  • Fall detection and controlled motor disable.
  • Mechanical hard stops on joints.
  • Initial testing with tether/overhead support and low current limits.
  • No autonomous operation around people until controlled, repeatable low-speed behaviour has been demonstrated.

22. Risk register

RiskMitigation
Actuators under-specified (torque, thermal)Bake-off and single-joint gate; size from twin torque traces with margin.
Mass overrunMass budget in CAD from datasheets; plan for ~25 kg.
Sim-to-real gapActuator system identification, domain randomisation, sim-to-sim checks (twin page).
Falls destroy hardwareGantry/tether, low current limits, sacrificial printed parts, mechanical hard stops.
Supplier quality or driftTest-part trial, incoming inspection, two qualified suppliers, revision-controlled drawings.
Scope creep (hands, 360° perception, voice)Freeze goals per phase; add capability only after its gate.
Locomotion harder than expectedRL walking inside a classical safety layer; reproduce a public humanoid baseline in sim first.
High-voltage safety (48 V class)Physical e-stop, contactor, precharge, fusing, insulated connectors, no live work.
Long timeline and motivationEach gate ends with a measured, demonstrable result.

23. Development phases

Timeline expectation (my judgement): roughly two to three years part-time to reliable tethered stepping; longer for free walking and the full perception/behaviour stack. There is no deadline, so the gates matter more than the calendar.
#PhaseDeliverableExit criterion
01Requirements + architectureFrozen height, DOF, payload, walking goals, power and safety requirementsSigned-off spec (§3)
02CAD + digital twinKinematic model, masses/inertias, MJCF, ROS interfacesStable sim control
03Actuator bake-off2–4 families tested: torque, backlash, thermals, noise, current, CAN reliabilityOne family selected on data
04Joint prototypeOne housing, manufactured and testedMatches the twin within thresholds
05Leg prototypeOne complete leg on the rigStiffness, wiring, calibration and control validated
06Lower bodyTwo legs + pelvis, emergency shutdownTethered standing and weight shift
07Full skeletonTorso, arms, head; hardware abstraction and calibration pipelineStable whole-body control
08WalkingStand → step → alternating steps → slow walk → turn → recoverySlow free walking
09PerceptionCameras, depth, IMU, people tracking, hand landmarks, world modelReal-time tracking on board
10Manipulation + behaviourPointing, reaching, following, gesture response, voice (grasping if hands exist)Defined task set executed
11ExteriorPanels, finish/anodising, sensor apertures, eyesFinal Hitmonlee form
12Rebuild packageFrozen BOM, CAD revisions, drawings, calibration procedures, containers, assembly notesRobot can be rebuilt or repaired from the package

24. What “done” means

Minimum

  • Stands unsupported for 10+ minutes and walks about 10 m slowly on a flat indoor floor.
  • Recovers from small pushes and stops safely on any fault.
  • Joint tracking error inside the limit set in stage A.
  • Tracks people and defined objects in real time on board (the render sheet suggests ≥30 FPS).
  • Recognises a defined set of hand signals (the render sheet suggests ≥90% accuracy) and orients head/body toward a person or target.
  • Points and reaches; grasps only if hands were added.
  • Fully disassembles; any failed part is replaced from the BOM; the robot can be rebuilt from the released package.

Stretch

  • Voice interaction, following, fetch tasks, walking on uneven floors, expressive eyes tied to behaviour.

25. First 30 days

WeekDo
1Set height/mass envelope, provisional ~24-DOF topology and the hands decision. Set up Ubuntu 24.04, ROS 2 Jazzy, MuJoCo and Playground; run a humanoid locomotion example.
2Build the skeleton in CAD; start the mass budget from actuator datasheets. Buy a desktop printer; print a scale leg and head mock-up.
3Export URDF, generate the MJCF, close the loop with mujoco_ros2_control. Implement FK/IK and basic joint control.
4Standing and stepping in simulation (classical stand, RL baseline). Write a per-joint actuator spec. Send one test part to 3–5 machining shops; request 2–3 actuator families for samples.
Day-30 deliverables: a runnable twin, a mass budget, an actuator spec sheet, printed fit-check parts, and test parts and samples on order.

27. Decisions and open questions

Working decisions (change any of these)

  • Personal project built to a professional standard; no deadline; not a cost play.
  • Body designed in CAD, made by suppliers (machined aluminium where it matters), assembled and tested by you.
  • Hitmonlee form; an exposed mechanical skeleton is acceptable during development.
  • Simulation first (MuJoCo/MJX, Isaac Sim secondary); ROS 2 Jazzy with ros2_control; a single joint before any bulk order.
  • Off-the-shelf integrated actuators chosen by bake-off, not a brand fixed now.
  • Hybrid manufacturing: print for fit-checks and non-structural parts, machine the structure.
  • RL for walking inside a classical safety layer.
  • Head: sensor bay kept separate from expressive display eyes.

Open

  • Assembly location (the original plan assumed Hong Kong; this affects shipping, import duty and inspection trips).
  • Final height and mass envelope.
  • Hands: gripper or gesture-only.
  • Printed versus machined arms.
  • Actuator family, after the bake-off.
  • Battery voltage and BMS.
  • Eye implementation and head shape.
  • Dev workstation GPU.
  • Shell material and finish.

28. Final recommendation

Do not start by buying anything large. The first physical deliverable is one excellent joint, not a Hitmonlee.

Each gate produces the information that decides whether the next stage deserves money and time. Reject an actuator that misses the torque-to-mass need before designing around it. Fix a housing that flexes before making a leg. Change the architecture if a leg cannot carry the target mass before ordering the rest.

Stop and re-plan if: no candidate actuator meets torque, thermal and mass needs; the twin cannot stand in simulation; or the calibrated twin and the bench still disagree after repeated system identification.

The differentiator is not the resemblance to Hitmonlee. It is that the whole machine is defined digitally, manufactured reproducibly, tested quantitatively, and can be built again.

29. Reference builds, code and videos

  • Berkeley Humanoid Lite (paper): open hardware, embedded code and RL training; roughly 0.8 m and 16 kg; printed cycloidal gearboxes; parts about $4,312 at US prices and $3,236 at China prices. Its locomotion is still rough.
  • AGILOped: open-source humanoid built on COTS QDD actuators.
  • MuJoCo Playground: GPU training in minutes; humanoid locomotion environments; sim-to-real shown on the Berkeley Humanoid, Unitree G1 and Booster T1.
  • mujoco_ros2_control demos: URDF-to-MJCF conversion, PID control and transmissions with ros2_control.
  • Unitree R1 as a commercial yardstick: $5,900, 121 cm, 25 kg, 24–26 DOF, no working hands.
  • Videos (not watched by me): Skyentific, simulation controlling a real robot arm; Skyentific, "How to build Humanoid: NVIDIA Isaac Lab, how to walk" (search the title); Berkeley Humanoid Lite build breakdown; I Built Humanoid Robot Legs; MathWorks, "The Walking Robot Problem" (RL Part 4, older, MATLAB-based).

DIGITAL TWIN

The robot is defined digitally before any hardware is ordered: one canonical model, simulated first, then checked against measured parts.

Contents

1. Role in the plan

The digital twin is the first stage of the spend sequence, and it sits between system architecture and engineering drawings in the manufacturing workflow. Nothing is machined until the twin exists and controllers have been shown to work in it.

Workflow position (Build plan §5.2) 
Requirements

   ↓

First spend gate (Build plan §20)
StageDigital twin
Spend target$0–300
GateStable kinematic/dynamic model and simulated control.

2. Simulators

2.1 Primary simulator: MuJoCo

Use MuJoCo as the first simulator. Its official Python bindings are maintained with the engine, and the package supports model construction, simulation, sensors, actuators and rendering. MJX extends MuJoCo with JAX/XLA execution on GPUs and other accelerators, which is useful for batched optimisation or reinforcement learning. MuJoCo Python documentation and MJX documentation.

2.2 Secondary simulator: NVIDIA Isaac Sim

Use Isaac Sim when photorealistic perception, synthetic camera data, richer environment simulation or NVIDIA ecosystem integration becomes useful. The current Isaac Sim documentation supports Python workflows, ROS 2 integration and repeatable Docker/headless deployments. The September 2026 release is 6.1.0. Isaac Sim documentation.

3. Simulation model

  • URDF/Xacro as the ROS-facing robot description.
  • MuJoCo MJCF generated/maintained from the canonical model.
  • Mass/inertia data derived from CAD.
  • Measured actuator torque-speed/current-temperature curves.
  • Joint limits and transmission ratios.
  • Contact/friction parameters.
  • Camera intrinsics/extrinsics.
  • IMU and force/contact sensor models.

4. Software touchpoints

Three ROS 2 packages carry the twin. The same robot description should work against real hardware and simulated hardware through ros2_control, so the twin is not a separate model that drifts from the robot.

ModuleRole in the twin
hitmonlee_descriptionURDF/Xacro, meshes, joint limits, transmissions, frames.
hitmonlee_simMuJoCo/MJX simulation and test environments.
hitmonlee_kinematicsFK/IK, Jacobians, body/foot transforms.

Full module list: Build plan §8.3 · back to §7

Control (Build plan §12)

  • Stage D — standing: use the simulator to find a stable posture and reproduce it on hardware.
  • RL-trained walking (MJX / MuJoCo Playground) is the primary route for stepping and walking, wrapped in a classical safety layer that the policy cannot override (Build plan §10).

First 30 days (Build plan §25, original numbering)

  1. Set a provisional 24-DOF kinematic topology.
  2. Build the robot skeleton in CAD.
  3. Export a URDF and create the MuJoCo model.
  4. Implement FK/IK and basic joint control in simulation.
  5. Build standing and stepping controllers in simulation.

6. Simulation stack and workstation

Simulation
┼─ MuJoCo
┼─ MJX / JAX
└─ NVIDIA Isaac Sim (secondary)

Use a Linux workstation with a capable NVIDIA GPU if possible. Isaac Sim is GPU-heavy; MuJoCo itself is much lighter (Build plan §17). Software stack in full: §26.

7. Validation: making the twin match the robot

A twin is only useful once it reproduces measured hardware. Define pass thresholds before testing, not after.

Measure on the benchGoes into the model as
Torque–speed and current curves, thermal deratingActuator force limits and speed limits
Friction and damping, rotor inertia (armature)Joint friction, damping and armature parameters
Backlash and complianceJoint-level tolerance and stiffness assumptions
Command-to-response latency over CANObservation and action delay, randomised in training
Link masses and centres of mass (weigh each assembly)Inertial properties replacing CAD estimates
Camera calibration and IMU alignmentSensor extrinsics and noise

Compare simulated and measured step responses for each joint, then for a leg, and update the model until the error is inside the thresholds you set.

8. Locomotion learning pipeline

  1. Run an existing humanoid environment in MuJoCo Playground to learn the workflow.
  2. Import your own MJCF, generated from the canonical URDF (mujoco_ros2_control demonstrates the conversion).
  3. Train with domain randomisation over friction, masses, joint offsets and latency.
  4. Check the policy in a second simulator (sim-to-sim), for example CPU MuJoCo or Isaac Lab.
  5. Deploy on the tether/gantry at low torque limits, then raise limits gradually.
  6. Keep the classical safety layer active throughout: joint, torque and thermal limits, watchdog, fall detection and motor disable.

9. Twin-to-hardware gates

GateTwin evidenceHardware evidence
Single jointModel of the chosen actuator with measured parametersStep, torque and thermal tests match the model within thresholds
LegLeg controlled in sim under loadSame motion on the rig; error logged
StandingStable posture found in simTethered standing, then unsupported
Stepping / walkingPolicy passes randomised sim-to-sim testsTethered steps, then slow free walking
